title: General Rules and Technical Recommendations for Tournaments

articles.heading: Playing Area Requirements
articles.content:
The playing area is the place where the games of a competition are played. The following standards apply:

Space: Sufficient space must be provided for all players to sit comfortably, with adequate distance between adjacent boards to prevent disturbance. Each player should have at least 60 cm of table width. For FIDE Top-Level Tournaments, the recommended minimum table size is 100 cm × 80 cm per board.

Lighting: Adequate, even lighting is essential. A minimum of 200 lux is recommended, with no direct light causing glare on the chessboards. Natural lighting should be supplemented or replaced by artificial lighting to ensure consistency.

Temperature and ventilation: The temperature should be maintained between 18°C and 24°C. Air conditioning or adequate ventilation must be provided. The playing hall should not be draughty.

Separation: The playing area must be separated from spectator areas, press areas, and analysis rooms. Physical barriers (ropes, partitions, or separate rooms) should prevent spectators from approaching the boards.

Noise: The playing area should be acoustically isolated from noise sources. Sound-dampening flooring (carpets or mats) is recommended.

For FIDE Top-Level Tournaments, additional requirements include: a separate room for players who have finished their games, a room for team captains in team events, and designated areas for Fair Play scanning.

articles.heading: Rest of the Playing Venue
articles.content:
The playing venue includes the playing area and all other designated areas. Minimum requirements are:

Toilets: Adequate toilet facilities must be accessible without players passing through the playing area of ongoing games. Where this is not possible, an arbiter should supervise access.

Analysis room: A separate analysis room should be provided where players who have finished their games can discuss completed games. This prevents disturbance of ongoing games.

Refreshments: A refreshment area should be available to players and officials. For long rounds (over 3 hours), water should be available in the playing area.

Smoking: A designated smoking area, in compliance with local laws, should be provided outside the playing area. The smoking area should, where possible, be supervised by an arbiter or assistant.

Medical facilities: At important events, first aid should be available. The Chief Arbiter should have contact information for emergency services.

Accreditation: Access to the playing area should be controlled. A clear accreditation system identifying players, arbiters, officials, press, and other authorised personnel is essential for large events.

The arbiter should inspect the entire playing venue before the start of the event and before each round to ensure all conditions are met.

articles.heading: Standards of Chess Equipment
articles.content:
FIDE sets mandatory standards for chess equipment used in rated events:

Chessboard:
- Square size: 50 mm to 65 mm (55–60 mm recommended)
- Light squares: white or cream
- Dark squares: green, brown, or dark grey
- Must not be shiny (to avoid reflections disturbing players)
- Algebraic notation coordinates are recommended on the border

Chess pieces (Staunton pattern or approved modern variation):
- King height: 85 mm to 105 mm (95 mm recommended)
- King base diameter: 40–50% of king height
- The pieces must be clearly distinguishable; the knight head must face to the right when placed on the board
- Material: wood preferred; plastic accepted

Colour of pieces:
- Light pieces: white, cream, or light-coloured
- Dark pieces: black, dark brown, or dark-coloured
- The contrast between light and dark pieces must be sufficient

Dimension matching: The king height and board square size must be compatible. As a guideline, the king's base diameter should cover 75–80% of a square.

For FIDE World Events and high-level Continental events, FIDE-approved equipment sets are required. The list of approved sets is maintained on the FIDE website.

articles.heading: FIDE-Compliant Electronic Chess Equipment
articles.content:
Electronic chess boards (e-boards) and digital clocks must be approved by FIDE to be used in rated events.

Electronic boards:
- Must accurately record all moves without human error
- Must transmit moves in real time for live broadcast in high-level events
- Must be able to detect piece placement accurately
- Must have a fail-safe mechanism if connection is lost
- If an electronic board malfunctions, the game may continue on a conventional board at the arbiter's discretion

Digital clocks:
- Must display time accurately to the nearest second
- Must support all required time control formats including increment (Fischer) and delay (Bronstein/Simple)
- Must have a clear, readable display visible to both players
- Must sound or show a clear signal when time expires (flag fall)
- Must support move counters where required

The list of FIDE-approved clocks and electronic boards is maintained on the FIDE website. In events where FIDE-approved equipment is required and an approved clock malfunctions, an arbiter-approved replacement must be used promptly.

Analogue clocks may only be used in events where the time control does not include an increment, and only with specific arbiter approval.

articles.heading: Clock Placement and Scoresheet Requirements
articles.content:
Clock placement:
- In individual tournaments, the clock is normally placed to the right of the player with the black pieces
- In team competitions, clocks typically face the same direction, and the arbiter must check that players do not press their neighbour's clock by mistake
- A player with a disability who would have difficulty with the standard clock position may request the clock be placed on the other side; this should be accommodated by rotating the board
- The arbiter has final authority on clock placement

Scoresheet requirements:
- Scoresheets must be provided to all players in all rated standard events
- The scoresheet must have spaces for: player names, date, round, result, and at least 60 move pairs
- Players must write legibly using standard algebraic notation (Appendix C of the Laws)
- The scoresheet belongs to the organiser and must be handed in at the end of the game
- Players may keep a copy of their scoresheet if the organiser provides carbon copy sheets
- Electronic scoresheets (certified by FIDE) may be used as alternatives to paper scoresheets

The Chief Arbiter should ensure an adequate supply of scoresheets is available before each round. Scoresheets should be pre-printed with the tournament name, round number, and board number where possible.
